ox: Incorrect. 0.42 is 2pq, the heterozygotes as a fraction of EVERYONE. The question asks only about people with the dominant phenotype, so the denominator must shrink to 0.91.
Incorrect. 0.49 is p², the homozygous dominant fraction of everyone. It is not the heterozygote share at all.
Incorrect. 0.21 is pq, half of 2pq. It comes from forgetting the 2 in 2pq (a heterozygote can arise two ways: A from mom/a from dad, or the reverse).
Correct. q² = 0.09, so q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. Heterozygotes 2pq = 2 × 0.7 × 0.3 = 0.42. Dominant phenotype = p² + 2pq = 0.49 + 0.42 = 0.91. Heterozygous among them = 0.42/0.91 = 42/91 = 6/13 ≈ 0.46.

p: At Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium the genotype frequencies are p² (dominant homozygotes), 2pq (heterozygotes) and q² (recessive homozygotes), and p + q = 1. You can only SEE the recessive phenotype directly, so start from it: q² is the recessive phenotype frequency.
When a question says 'among people with the dominant phenotype', you must divide by that group's size (p² + 2pq = 1 − q²), not by the whole population.

x1C_114.trap: Answering 0.42 (carriers as a fraction of everyone) when the question asks about carriers among dominant-phenotype people.
x1C_114.eli: Imagine 100 kids and 9 show the rare trait. That tells you q² = 9/100, so q = 3/10. Then you build the rest of the crowd from p = 7/10.
mem: Start from the one you can SEE: recessive phenotype = q².
'Among the dominant phenotype' → divide by 1 − q², not by 1.

fm.f: p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p = frequency of the dominant allele, q = frequency of the recessive allele, q² = recessive homozygotes, 2pq = heterozygotes, p² = dominant homozygotes
fm.why: We use Hardy–Weinberg because it turns the one frequency we can observe (q²) into every genotype frequency.

x1C_114.sc: Perfect squares do the work: 0.09 = 0.3², so q = 0.3 and p = 0.7. No calculator needed.
x1C_114.mn: p² = Pure dominant, 2pq = Pass-along carriers, q² = Quiet recessive (the one you can see).

ox: Correct. Type A blood is Iᴬ Iᴬ or Iᴬ i. Fraction = p² + 2pr = 0.3² + 2 × 0.3 × 0.6 = 0.09 + 0.36 = 0.45.
Incorrect. 0.09 is only the Iᴬ Iᴬ homozygotes. Type A also includes Iᴬ i people, who have the A phenotype because Iᴬ is dominant to i.
Incorrect. 0.36 is only the Iᴬ i heterozygotes (2pr). It leaves out the Iᴬ Iᴬ people, who are also type A.
Incorrect. 0.30 is the ALLELE frequency of Iᴬ, not the frequency of the blood type. People can carry Iᴬ and still be type AB, and the A phenotype also comes from two copies.

concept.t: ABO blood types from allele frequencies
p: Three alleles (Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i) give six genotypes and four phenotypes. Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant with each other, and both are dominant to i. If p, q and r are the frequencies of Iᴬ, Iᴮ and i, then type A = p² + 2pr, type B = q² + 2qr, type AB = 2pq and type O = r².

x1C_087.trap: Counting only Iᴬ Iᴬ (0.09) or confusing the allele frequency 0.3 with the phenotype frequency.
x1C_087.eli: Type A people are everyone who carries at least one A and no B: the AA people plus the A-and-O people.
mem: Type A = IᴬIᴬ + Iᴬi; type B = IᴮIᴮ + Iᴮi; AB = IᴬIᴮ; O = ii.
Type O is the only one you can read straight from an allele: O = r².

fm.f: Type A = p² + 2pr, where p = frequency of Iᴬ, r = frequency of i, p² = Iᴬ Iᴬ people, 2pr = Iᴬ i people
fm.why: We add both genotypes that give the A phenotype because Iᴬ is dominant over i.

x1C_087.sc: Type A + type O = (p + r)². So type A = (p + r)² − r² = 0.9² − 0.6² = 0.81 − 0.36 = 0.45.
x1C_087.mn: O is 'ii' (needs two recessives), so O = r². Everything else adds the dominant-carrying genotypes.
